body.text: In short:
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has concluded its inquiries into allegations of misleading food labelling aired by Four Corners.
The watchdog says it found no evidence of misleading labelling on processed tomato products and cage-free eggs, after reviewing the businesses' supply chain processes and controls.
Source Certain, the independent laboratory that tested dozens of food products for Four Corners, says it is "disappointed" the ACCC did not conduct its own independent testing.
Australia's consumer watchdog says it has concluded its inquiries into allegations of food fraud aired by Four Corners, finding no evidence of misleading labelling on two types of food products.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said its inquiries focused on the origin of processed tomato products and allegedly false "cage-free" claims for eggs.

As part of its inquiries, the ACCC said it "obtained and examined traceability material to trace the origin of the impugned products identified in the program", but did not conduct independent testing.
"The ACCC did not find evidence that the country of origin or cage-free claims made on food labels in relation to the tomato and egg products were false or misleading,"

Source Certain, the independent laboratory that conducted forensic testing of food products for Four Corners, said it was "disappointed the ACCC limited its inquiry to two products, and its reliance on evidence supplied by the companies and suppliers whose products were under investigation".
The spokesperson also said Source Certain was disappointed the watchdog had not commissioned any independent forensic testing to verify the companies' and suppliers' claims.
"Some of the biggest food fraud cases in the world involved products with near-perfect paperwork," the spokesperson for Source Certain said.
"In the 2013 horse meat scandal, the documents said beef and testing showed it wasn't. The paperwork alone would never have found it."
Four Corners food fraud investigation
As part of a months-long investigation, Four Corners collated thousands of food import inspection records, national food recalls, state regulatory records and international food fraud intelligence.

Forensic testing from Source Certain, commissioned for the program, found dozens of tomato paste products that claimed to be from Australia or Italy had chemical profiles consistent with Chinese-grown tomatoes.
The testing revealed some seafood supplied to the food services sector and promoted as Australian, such as white fish and prawns, was consistent with being sourced from Vietnam.
It tested 11 brands of turmeric and detected signs of adulteration in three brands.

The investigation also tested six spirits purchased from licensed bottle shops in Melbourne, finding all exceeded legal methanol limits, with three recording levels more than eight times the permitted limit.
Source Certain also tested 20 brands of eggs across four states, and found some caged eggs marketed as "cage-free" in one brand in one state did not match those claims following repeated tests.
ACCC focused on tomato products and eggs

In response to the allegations, the ACCC said it conducted inquiries into potentially misleading consumer conduct regarding the processed tomato products and eggs by reviewing the businesses' supply chain processes, and controls to support country of origin and cage-free claims.

"We obtained and examined traceability material to trace the origin of the impugned products identified in the program, and details of relevant audits and certifications," an ACCC spokesperson told Four Corners.

"The ACCC also obtained and examined details of food provenance testing results from Source Certain, and testing by … accredited laboratories commissioned by each of the suppliers of processed tomato products identified in the program."

The watchdog also said it engaged with state and territory food regulators and food manufacturers, as well as the National Measurement Institute, the Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation and Food Standards Australia New Zealand.

The ACCC spokesperson said it did not examine other issues raised by Four Corners relating to Australia's health star rating system, turmeric or illicit alcohol, as it deemed those concerns outside the ACCC's remit.
"While food origin testing can show whether a sample is consistent with a certain origin, such testing cannot prove origin with certainty," ACCC commissioner Luke Woodward said.
"In our inquiries, we have considered testing, together with supply chain documentation and other evidence produced by suppliers to substantiate their food origin claims."
The ACCC said there were a range of ways to test where a food product came from that could provide "strong evidence to support origin claims".
However, it said no single test could be relied upon as a definitive or standalone means of determining origin.
"It was important to examine these allegations, because such claims matter to consumers," Mr Woodward said.
"When shopping for groceries, consumers must be able to rely on the accuracy of claims made on labels, packaging and in advertising about the products they may wish to buy."
More resources needed to tackle food crime, says Source Certain
A Source Certain spokesperson said these investigations were "complex and demand significant time and resources".
"That's why many jurisdictions, including the UK after the horse meat scandal, now have dedicated food crime enforcement teams," the spokesperson said.

"As practitioners with extensive experience in this supply chain investigation area, we'd encourage investigations to go further: supply chain mapping, commodity flow analysis, and intelligence from people inside the chain.
"Some of these chains are long and opaque. It's challenging work, and that difficulty is a big part of why fraud in global supply chains remains as widespread as it is."
An ABC spokesperson said the organisation stood by the Four Corners investigation.
"Source Certain is a leading global provider of origin verification services," the spokesperson said.
"It conducted extensive, independent blind testing of a wide range of food products and stands by its testing.
"The ABC also stands by the rigour of the testing and how Four Corners reported the findings."
The spokesperson also said the ACCC had identified no specific flaw in Source Certain's testing.
"The ACCC looked at two foods in what was a much broader investigation," they said.
"The integrity of Australia's food supply is a matter of significant public interest and Four Corners revealed concerning issues that are deserving of proper scrutiny."
